C1.quote: I decided that there should be no undefined result values in L – instead, exceptions should always be raised when no correct return value can be computed.
C1.statement: When no correct value can be computed, raise an exception; never return an undefined value or let an error pass silently.

C2.quote: In L, all objects that can be named are said to be "first class."
C2.statement: Every object that can be named has equal status: it can be assigned, passed, returned and stored like any other.

C3.quote: A major design constraint was that I didn't want to add syntax for methods that differed from the syntax for functions.
C3.statement: Prefer the minimal solution that reuses existing mechanisms; do not add new syntax when an existing construct will serve.

C4.quote: In L, variables are simply names that refer to objects.
C4.statement: Variables are names that refer to objects, needing no declaration; all type checking happens at run time.

C5.quote: One of the rules I took from the predecessor was that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that was a valid input to the language's parser.
C5.statement: Every value, when printed or converted to a string, should read back as a valid expression to the parser.

C6.quote: I decided to generalize these to a common concept, the sequence.
C6.statement: Generalize related types to a common concept so core operations work the same on all of them.

C7.quote: the predecessor-inspired philosophy of not requiring users to care about a uninteresting implementation details
C7.statement: Do not require users to care about uninteresting implementation details.
